item.title: Mark Ramseyer
item.description:
Mark Ramseyer

Mitsubishi Professor of Japanese Legal Studies

Mark Ramseyer spent most of his childhood in provincial towns and cities in southern Japan, attending Japanese schools for K-6. He returned to the U.S. for college. Before attending law school, he studied Japanese history in graduate school. Ramseyer graduated from HLS in 1982. He clerked for the Hon. Stephen Breyer (then on the First Circuit), worked for two years at Sidley & Austin (in corporate tax), and studied as a Fulbright student at the University of Tokyo. After teaching at UCLA and the University of Chicago, he came to Harvard in 1998. He has also taught or co-taught courses at several Japanese universities (in Japanese). In his research, Ramseyer primarily studies Japanese law, and primarily from a law & economics perspective. In addition to a variety of Japanese law courses, he teaches the basic Corporations course. With Professors Klein and Bainbridge, he co-edits a Foundation Press casebook in the field.

item.title: Mark Schelker
item.description:
Mark Schelker

Professor of Economics, University of Fribourg

Mark is a professor of economics at the University of Fribourg. He mostly works in political economics and public economics. He is interested in how political institutions affect political, economic and social outcomes, and how economic and political networks interact over time and space.

item.title: Matthew Baum
item.description:
Matthew Baum

Marvin Kalb Professor of Global Communications and Professor of Public Policy, HKS

Email: matthew_baum@harvard.edu

Matthew A. Baum is Marvin Kalb Professor of Global Communications and Professor of Public Policy at Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government. His research focuses on “delineating the effects of domestic politics on international conflict and cooperation” generally and American foreign policy specifically, as well as the role of mass media and public opinion in contemporary American politics. His work has appeared in over a dozen leading scholarly journals, including the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, and Journal of Politics. His books include Soft News Goes to War: Public Opinion and American Foreign Policy in the New Media Age and War Stories: The Causes and Consequences of Public Views of War (Forthcoming 2009, Princeton University Press). He has contributed op/ed articles to various newspapers and magazines in the U.S. and abroad. Before coming to Harvard, Baum was associate professor of political science and communication studies at UCLA. He received his PhD in political science at UC San Diego in 2000.

item.title: Matthew Blackwell
item.description:
Matthew Blackwell

Associate Professor of Government, FAS

Email: mblackwell@gov.harvard.edu

Matthew Blackwell is an Associate Professor of Government at Harvard University. He studies political methodology, focusing on “dynamic causal inference, instrumental variables, experimental design, missing data, and panel data.” His substantive interests include “the lasting effects of slavery on political attitudes in the US South.”

item.title: Matthew Stephenson
item.description:
Matthew Stephenson

Eli Goldston Professor of Law

Matthew Stephenson is Eli Goldston Professor of Law at Harvard Law School, where he teaches administrative law, legislation and regulation, and political economy of public law. His research focuses on applying positive political theory to public law, especially administrative procedure, judicial institutions, and separation of powers. Before joining Harvard Law School’s faculty, he clerked for Senior Judge Stephen Williams on the D.C. Circuit and for Justice Anthony Kennedy on the Supreme Court. He received his J.D. and Ph.D. in political science from Harvard in 2003 and his B.A. from Harvard College in 1997.

item.title: Max Bazerman
item.description:
Max Bazerman

Jesse Isidor Straus Professor of Business Administration, Harvard Business School

Email: mbazerman@hbs.edu

Max H. Bazerman holds the Jesse Isidor Straus Professorship of Business Administration at Harvard Business School and serves as Co-Director of the Center for Public Leadership at Harvard Kennedy School.

His research centers on decision making, negotiation, and ethics. He has authored, co-authored, or co-edited twenty books, including The Power of Noticing (Simon and Schuster, 2014) and Blind Spots (with Ann Tenbrunsel, Princeton University Press, 2011), along with over 200 research articles and chapters. He serves on editorial boards of multiple journals including American Behavioral Scientist, Journal of Management and Governance, Mind and Society, and others.

item.title: Maya Sen
item.description:
Maya Sen

Professor of Public Policy, Kennedy School

Maya Sen is a political scientist and Professor of Public Policy at Harvard University. Her research interests include law, political economy, race and ethnic politics, and statistical methods. Her research has been published in journals such as the American Political Science Review, the American Journal of Political Science, and the Journal of Politics, and has been covered by the New York Times, the Washington Post, The Economist, National Public Radio, and other outlets.

item.title: Melani Cammett
item.description:
Melani Cammett

Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs, Department of Government; Professor in the Department of Global Health and Population, Chan School of Public Health

Email: mcammett@gov.harvard.edu

Melani Cammett is Professor of Government at Harvard University, specializing in the political economy of development and the Middle East and North Africa. She has authored four books:

  • A Political Economy of the Middle East (with Ishac Diwan, Alan Richards, and John Waterbury, 2015)
  • Compassionate Communalism: Welfare and Sectarianism in Lebanon (2014), which won the 2015 APSA Giovanni Sartori Book Award and received Honorable Mention for the 2015 APSA Gregory Luebbert Book Award
  • The Politics of Nonstate Welfare (coedited with Lauren Morris MacLean, 2014)
  • Globalization and Business Politics in North Africa: A Comparative Perspective (2007, 2010)

She has received fellowships from organizations including the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Qualitative and Multi-Methods Research Section of APSA, the Comparative Politics Section of APSA, the Smith Richardson Foundation, the U.S. Institute of Peace, the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies, and the Social Science Research Council. She has “published numerous articles in scholarly and policy journals, and consults for development policy organizations.”

item.title: Melissa Dell
item.description:
Melissa Dell

Professor of Economics, Department of Economics

Melissa Dell is a professor in the Economics Department and a faculty research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. Her research focuses on long-run economic development, primarily in Latin America and Asia. She has examined the impacts of weather on economic growth and is currently conducting research about the long-run effects of agrarian reform and agricultural technology investments in Mexico and East Asia. She received a PhD in Economics from MIT, a masters degree in Economics from Oxford, and a BA from Harvard College.

item.title: Michael Hiscox
item.description:
Michael Hiscox

Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs

Michael J. Hiscox is the Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs at Harvard University. He earned his B. Econ. (First Class Honours) from the University of Sydney in 1989 and his Ph.D in Government from Harvard in 1997. He served as Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC San Diego from 1997 to 2001, then held the John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Social Sciences position at Harvard from 2001 to 2005.

item.title: Michael Kremer
item.description:
Michael Kremer

Gates Professor of Developing Societies

Michael Kremer is the Gates Professor of Developing Societies in the Department of Economics at Harvard University and Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a recipient of a MacArthur Fellowship and a Presidential Faculty Fellowship, and was named a Young Global Leader by the World Economic Forum. His recent research focuses on “education and health in developing countries, immigration, and globalization.” He and Rachel Glennerster co-authored Strong Medicine: Creating Incentives for Pharmaceutical Research on Neglected Diseases.

item.title: Michael P. Brenner
item.description:
Michael P. Brenner

Michael F. Cronin Professor of Applied Mathematics and Applied Physics and Professor of Physics

Email: brenner@seas.harvard.edu

His research group uses applied mathematics methods to address scientific and engineering problems. They are described as “first and foremost problem solvers” who search for problems where mathematics can answer scientific questions.

Over the past decade, the research has focused on theoretical modeling in physical sciences and engineering, much of it arising from close contact with experimentalists. Problems addressed include “the breaking of fluid droplets; sonoluminescence (the production of light from small bubbles)” as well as sedimentation of small particles, device design, and electrospinning.

item.title: Michael Porter
item.description:
Michael Porter

Bishop William Lawrence University Professor

Michael E. Porter

Bishop William Lawrence University Professor

Michael Porter is an economist, researcher, author, advisor, speaker and teacher. Throughout his career at Harvard Business School, he has brought economic theory and strategy concepts to bear on many of the most challenging problems facing corporations, economies and societies, including market competition and company strategy, economic development, the environment, and health care. His extensive research is widely recognized in governments, corporations, NGOs, and academic circles around the globe. His research has received numerous awards, and he is the most cited scholar today in economics and business. While Dr. Porter is, at the core, a scholar, his work has also achieved remarkable acceptance by practitioners across multiple fields.

item.title: Michael Wilson
item.description:
Michael Wilson

Instructor in Emergency Medicine, HMS

Michael Wilson received his M.D. from the University of Michigan and his Ph.D. in Health Economics from Johns Hopkins University in 2010. He is a board certified Emergency Physician at Brigham and Women’s Hospital with fellowship training in Trauma and Critical Care Medicine and an Instructor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School. His research interests focus on measuring the value of emergency department care. At the broadest level, he seeks to develop a measure of emergency department performance along both quality and cost dimensions. His research projects examine variations in quality and cost and disparities by race, gender, and socioeconomic status for cohorts of patients who present to emergency departments for care. The goal of this research is to provide an evidence base for the construction of ED-specific value-based incentives for physicians and hospitals.

item.title: Michele Lamont
item.description:
Michele Lamont

Robert I. Goldman Professor of European Studies

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Mina Cikara
item.description:
Mina Cikara

Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology

Professor Cikara studies “how the mind, brain, and behavior change when the social context shifts from ‘me and you’ to ‘us and them.’” Her primary focus is on how group membership, competition, and prejudice disrupt empathy and the ability to see others as human. She employs diverse methodological tools including “standard laboratory experiments, implicit and explicit behavioral measures, fMRI and psychophysiology” to investigate failures of empathy, dehumanization, and intergroup misunderstanding. She is also interested in behavioral outcomes of these processes, particularly “willingness to harm out-group members.”

item.title: Naijia Liu
item.description:
Naijia Liu

Assistant Professor, Department of Government

Naijia is a political methodologist with “a broad interest on quantitative methods on social sciences.” She works on projects involving missing data imputation, text analysis/NLP, and social media studies.

item.title: Neil Shephard
item.description:
Neil Shephard

Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science

Neil Shephard has been Professor of Economics and of Statistics at Harvard University since 2013. He holds a B.A. in Economics and Statistics (first class awarded with distinction) from the University of York and a M.Sc. in Statistics (awarded with distinction) and Ph.D. from the London School of Economics (LSE). He previously was a faculty member at the LSE and Nuffield College, Oxford University. His research interests are mainly focused on theoretical and applied econometrics and statistics. He has been a leader in the development of the econometrics of stochastic volatility as well as simulation based inference. He is credited with important contributions to the development in sequential learning (e.g. the auxiliary particle filter). He is currently focusing on non-parametric Bayesian methods, simulation, high frequency finance and valuing income contingent student loans. During his time at Oxford University he cofounded the Masters in Financial Economics and founded the interdisciplinary Oxford-Man Institute, which he directed from 2007-2011. He is an emeritus fellow at Nuffield College, Oxford, a Fellow of the Econometric Society, a Fellow of the British Academy and received an honorary doctorate in economics from Aarhus University. He was awarded the Richard Stone Prize in Applied Econometrics in 2012.

item.title: Nima Hejazi
item.description:
Nima Hejazi

Assistant Professor of Biostatistics

Dr. Hejazi’s research combines causal inference and machine learning, aiming to develop “tailored, assumption-lean statistical procedures for efficient and robust inference about scientifically informative” parameters. He is driven by methodological challenges in “robust non- and semi-parametric inference, high-dimensional inference, targeted loss-based estimation, and biased sampling designs.” His statistical work is informed by collaboration in clinical trials and computational biology, particularly regarding “vaccine efficacy and drug treatment trials, infectious disease epidemiology, and immunology.” He is also interested in high-performance statistical computing and open source software development for reproducible applied statistics.

item.title: Peter Bol
item.description:
Peter Bol

Charles H. Carswell Professor of East Asian Languages and Civilizations, Harvard University

Peter Bol is a scholar of Chinese intellectual and cultural history. His research focuses on the history of China’s cultural elites, both nationally and locally, spanning the 7th to 17th centuries. He also works extensively in geospatial analysis and digital humanities projects related to Chinese history.

He authored “This Culture of Ours”: Intellectual Transitions in T’ang and Sung China, Neo-Confucianism in History, and Localizing Learning: The Literati Enterprise in Wuzhou, 1100-1600.

item.title: Peter V. Marsden
item.description:
Peter V. Marsden

Edith and Benjamin Geisinger Professor of Sociology

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Pia Raffler
item.description:
Pia Raffler

Assistant Professor of Government

Pia Raffler is an Assistant Professor in Political Science at Harvard University. She studies the politics of development, focusing on “governance, bureaucracy, and electoral politics in Sub-Saharan Africa.” Her research examines political oversight of bureaucrats and its implications for public service provision, as well as electoral behavior. She “works closely with government agencies to understand impediments to accountable representation, often through large-scale field experiments.” She holds a PhD from Yale University and a Master from Columbia University and is an EGAP member.

item.title: Rafaella Sadun
item.description:
Rafaella Sadun

Professor, Harvard Business School

Raffaella Sadun is a Professor at the Harvard Business School. Her research centers on “the economics of productivity, management and organizational change,” documenting economic and cultural determinants of managerial choices and their implications for organizational performance across private and public sectors, including healthcare and education. She co-founded the World Management Survey and the Executive Time Use Study. Her work has been published in leading journals such as the American Economic Review, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Economic Journal, and covered by major outlets including The New York Times, The Economist, The Wall Street Journal, and the Financial Times. She holds affiliations as a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Faculty Associate at the Centre for Economic Performance at LSE, Research Affiliate at the Center for Economic Policy Research, and Research Associate in the Ariadne Labs Program at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. In 2012 she “was nominated as a Junior Faculty Fellow at the Kauffman Foundation.”

item.title: Rajarshi Mukherjee
item.description:
Rajarshi Mukherjee

Assistant Professor, Department of Biostatistics

Rajarshi Mukherjee’s research focuses on “causal inference from observational studies using non-parametric methods, sparse signal detection problems in genomics, and networks analysis” with applications in neural spike train analysis.

item.title: Ramana Nanda
item.description:
Ramana Nanda

Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration

Ramana Nanda is the Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration and Co-Director of the Private Capital Project at Harvard Business School. His research focuses on “financing frictions facing new ventures,” aiming to help entrepreneurs with fundraising and to illuminate how “financial intermediaries, corporate R&D and policy makers can improve the odds of selecting and commercializing the most promising ideas and technologies in the economy.”

item.title: Reshmaan N Hussam
item.description:
Reshmaan N Hussam

Assistant Professor of Business Administration

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Richard Wrangham
item.description:
Richard Wrangham

Ruth Moore Professor of Biological Anthropology, Emeritus

Richard Wrangham is the Ruth Moore Professor of Biological Anthropology, Emeritus. He “received a Ph.D. in Zoology from Cambridge University, where he studied under the renowned ethologist Robert Hinde.” He served on faculty in departments of Anthropology, Psychology and Biology at institutions including Bristol University, Stanford University, King’s College Cambridge, and the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.

item.title: Richard Zeckhauser
item.description:
Richard Zeckhauser

Frank Plumpton Ramsey Professor of Political Economy

Richard J. Zeckhauser is the Frank Plumpton Ramsey Professor of Political Economy at Harvard University John F. Kennedy School of Government. He pursues a blend of conceptual and applied research. He believes society’s primary challenge is allocating resources according to citizens’ preferences. Much of his conceptual work explores possibilities for democratic, decentralized allocation procedures. His ongoing policy work examines ways to promote human health, help labor and financial markets function more efficiently, and support informed choices by individuals and government agencies. His current major research focuses on “the performance of institutions confronted with inadequate commitment capabilities, incomplete information flow and human participants who fail to behave” according to rational models (such as engaging in herd behavior). Financial markets and health risks serve as the subjects of his major empirical investigations.

item.title: Robert Bates
item.description:
Robert Bates

Eaton Professor of the Science of Government, Emeritus

Email: robert.bates.harvard.edu@gmail.com

Robert H. Bates is Eaton Professor in the Department of Government and a member of the Department of African and African-American Studies. He has also served as Professeur associé in the Department of Economics at the University of Toulouse. After rising to Full Professor at the California Institute of Technology, he became the Henry R. Luce Professor of Political Science and Economics at Duke University, where he also directed its Center for Political Economy.

item.title: Robert Sampson
item.description:
Robert Sampson

Henry Ford II Professor of the Social Sciences

Robert J. Sampson is Henry Ford II Professor of the Social Sciences at Harvard University, where he was appointed in 2003. Before that he taught for twelve years in the Department of Sociology at the University of Chicago and for seven years at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Sampson was a Senior Research Fellow at the American Bar Foundation from 1994-2002, and in the 1997-98 and 2002-03 academic years he was a Fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences in Stanford, California. In 2005, he received a three-year RWJ Investigator Award in Health Policy Research and was inducted as a Fellow into the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

item.title: Ryan Enos
item.description:
Ryan Enos

Professor, Department of Government

Ryan D. Enos is a Professor of Government and Faculty Associate in the Institute for Quantitative Social Science specializing in American Politics, Political Psychology, and Race and Ethnic Politics. He studies political behavior and intergroup attitudes through “laboratory and field experiments and other methods.” He directs the Working Group in Political Psychology, described as “an interdisciplinary forum for research on the microfoundations of citizen and elite behavior,” as well as the Harvard Digital Lab for the Social Sciences. His research has appeared in publications including the American Political Science Review, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and the American Journal of Political Science, and “has been covered in major media outlets such as the New York Times and the Washington Post.” He earned his AB in political science and history from U.C. Berkeley and his MA and PhD in political science from UCLA. Before entering academia, “he was a teacher at Paul Robeson High School in Chicago, IL.”

item.title: Salil Vadhan
item.description:
Salil Vadhan

Vicky Joseph Professor of Computer Science

Salil Vadhan is the Vicky Joseph Professor of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics in the Harvard University School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, and the Director of the Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society. He earned his PhD in Applied Mathematics from MIT in 1999 and served as an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow at MIT and the Institute for Advanced Study before joining Harvard’s faculty in 2001. His awards include “a Simons Investigator Award, a Godel Prize, a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Phi Beta Kappa Award for Excellence in Teaching, and the ACM Doctoral Dissertation Award.”

item.title: Sebastian Bauhoff
item.description:
Sebastian Bauhoff

Assistant Professor of Global Health and Economics, HSPH

Email: sbauhoff@hsph.harvard.edu

Sebastian Bauhoff is an Assistant Professor of Global Health and Economics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and an affiliate of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science. His research focuses on “innovations in health care financing and service delivery that can increase access, efficiency and quality of care in low and middle-income countries.”

item.title: Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez
item.description:
Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez

Bluhm Family Assistant Professor of Data Science and Education

Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez is the Bluhm Family Assistant Professor of Data Science and Education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. He earned his doctorate in Sociology of Education from Stanford University’s Graduate School of Education. As a sociologist of science, he employs computational linguistics and network analysis to examine how research agendas evolve over time. More recently, he has shifted his focus toward “the study of adolescent experience, college admissions, and technologies of belonging.” His research has appeared in the American Sociological Review, the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science, and American Educational Research Journal.

item.title: Sharon-Lise Normand
item.description:
Sharon-Lise Normand

S. James Adelstein Professor of Health Care Policy

Sharon-Lise T. Normand, PhD, holds the S. James Adelstein Professorship of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School and is a Professor in Biostatistics at Harvard’s School of Public Health. Her research centers on developing statistical methods for health services research, with a primary emphasis on Bayesian approaches. Her work encompasses quality of care assessment, causal inference methods, provider profiling, meta-analysis, and latent variable modeling. She has built an extensive research program analyzing treatment patterns and care quality for cardiovascular disease and mental disorder patients.

item.title: Stephen Ansolabehere
item.description:
Stephen Ansolabehere

Frank G. Thompson Professor of Government

Email: sda@gov.harvard.edu

Stephen Ansolabehere is Frank G. Thompson Professor of Government at Harvard University. He specializes in public opinion and elections, with extensive publications on elections, mass media, representation, political economy, and public opinion (particularly regarding energy and the environment).

He authored five books: Cheap and Clean, The Media Game, Going Negative, American Government, and The End of Inequality.

item.title: Steven Currall
item.description:
Steven Currall

Executive Director, Academic-Corporate Initiatives, OVPR

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Suzanne Preston Blier
item.description:
Suzanne Preston Blier

Allen Whitehill Clowes Professor of Fine Arts and of African and African American Studies

Email: blier@fas.harvard.edu

Suzanne Preston Blier earned her Ph.D. in 1981 from Columbia and holds the Allen Whitehill Clowes Professor of Fine Arts and of African and African American Studies position at Harvard University. She is a historian of African art and architecture working in both the History of Art and Architecture and African and African American Studies Departments, and is a member of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science.

item.title: SV Subramanian
item.description:
SV Subramanian

Professor of Population Health and Geography

S (“Subu”) V Subramanian is a Professor of Population Health and Geography at the Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard Chan School of Public Health, and a senior core faculty at the Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies. He is also the founding director for an interdisciplinary PhD program in Population Health Sciences that is currently being developed at Harvard. He received his under- and post-graduate training at the University of Delhi, and completed his PhD in geography from the University of Portsmouth, UK in 2000. Subu has published over 425 articles, book chapters, and books in the field of social and contextual determinants of health, health inequalities in India with a special emphasis on nutritional inequalities among children and adults, and applied multilevel statistical models. He has co-edited 2 books titled Global Perspectives on Social Capital and Health and Social Capital and Health. Subu was the first to develop a course on the concept and application of multilevel statistical methods at Harvard, which he has been successfully teaching at Harvard Chan since 2001, as well as around the world. He has advised over 100 masters, doctoral and postdoctoral students as mentor, academic advisor and dissertation committee member. Subu has served as a permanent member of the National Institutes of Health Community Influences on Health Behavior (CIHB) Study Section, and as reviewer for several national and international funding agencies. He is the Editor-in-Chief (along with Ichiro Kawachi) for the international journal Social Science & Medicine (SSM), in addition to being a Senior Editor for the social epidemiology office of SSM. He is an editorial consultant to The Lancet, an international advisory board member for the Lancet Global Health, and serves as an academic editor to PLoS Medicine, besides serving as an editorial board member of several journals.

item.title: Timothy Colton
item.description:
Timothy Colton

Morris and Anna Feldberg Professor of Government and Russian Studies

Timothy J. Colton is Morris and Anna Feldberg Professor of Government and Russian Studies and the Chair of the Department of Government. His main interest is Russian and post-Soviet government and politics.

He authored The Dilemma of Reform in the Soviet Union (1986); Moscow: Governing the Socialist Metropolis (1995), which was “named best scholarly book in government and political science by the Association of American Publishers”; Transitional Citizens: Voters and What Influences Them in the New Russia (2000); and Popular Choice and Managed Democracy: The Russian Elections of 1999 and 2000 (with Michael McFaul, 2003). At the time of this profile, he was writing a book on Boris Yeltsin’s statecraft and coordinating a joint project on the post-Communist state.

item.title: Tomiko Brown-Nagin
item.description:
Tomiko Brown-Nagin

Daniel P.S. Paul Professor of Constitutional Law; Professor of History, Faculty of Arts and Sciences

Email: tbrownnagin@law.harvard.edu

Tomiko Brown-Nagin is described as “an award-winning legal historian and expert in constitutional law and education law and policy.” She has published in numerous prestigious journals including the Yale Law Journal, Columbia Law Review, Duke Law Journal, and Journal of Law & Education, covering topics such as equal protection jurisprudence, civil rights law and history, the Affordable Care Act, and education reform.

item.title: Torben Iversen
item.description:
Torben Iversen

Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy

Torben Iversen is Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy in the Government Department at Harvard University. His research and teaching interests include comparative political economy, electoral politics, and applied formal theory. He is the author or co-author of Big Data and the Welfare State: How the Information Revolution Threatens Social Solidarity (Cambridge UP 2022) (with Philipp Rehm), Democracy and Prosperity: Reinventing Capitalism through a Turbulent Century (Princeton UP 2019) (with David Soskice), Women, Work, and Politics: The Political Economy of Gender Inequality (Yale UP 2010) (with Frances Rosenbluth), Capitalism, Democracy, and Welfare (Cambridge UP 2005), and Contested Economic Institutions (Cambridge UP 1999). He has also authored or co-authored “more than four dozen articles on comparative politics and political economy.” He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has held fellowships including Radcliffe Fellow, Guggenheim Fellow, Hoover National Fellow, and “a BP Centennial Professor at the London School of Economics.”

item.title: Tyler VanderWeele
item.description:
Tyler VanderWeele

John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology

Tyler J. VanderWeele is the John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology in the Departments of Epidemiology and Biostatistics at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, and director of the Human Flourishing Program and co-director of the Initiative on Health, Religion and Spirituality at Harvard University. He holds degrees from the University of Oxford, University of Pennsylvania, and Harvard University in mathematics, philosophy, theology, finance, and biostatistics. His methodological research focuses on “theory and methods for distinguishing between association and causation in the biomedical and social sciences” and more recently on psychosocial measurement theory. His empirical research spans psychiatric and social epidemiology; the science of happiness and flourishing; and the study of religion and health. He received the 2017 Presidents’ Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies (COPSS). He has published over three hundred papers in peer-reviewed journals and is author of the books Explanation in Causal Inference (2015), Modern Epidemiology (2021), and Measuring Well-Being (2021). He also writes a monthly blog posting on topics related to human flourishing for Psychology Today.

item.title: Vesall Nourani
item.description:
Vesall Nourani

Assistant Professor, Harvard Graduate School of Education

Vesall Nourani is an assistant professor at HGSE. His research explores “the roles of knowledge and learning in economic activity across sub-Saharan Africa.” He conducts research on educational programs promoting community-based research, investigation, and dialogue aimed at advancing community development. His current projects use randomized controlled trials and other causal inference tools to study program impacts in Uganda and Colombia.

item.title: Vincent Pons
item.description:
Vincent Pons

Associate Professor, Harvard Business School

He is “an Associate Professor at Harvard Business School” and affiliated with NBER and J-PAL.

His research focuses on understanding why representative democracies sometimes fail to produce leaders and policies that match citizens’ preferences.

His work has been published in top journals including Econometrica, the American Economic Review, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the American Political Science Review, with media coverage in outlets like The New York Times and The Economist.

item.title: Walid Yassin
item.description:
Walid Yassin

Instructor in Psychiatry, HMS

Dr. Yassin works at the crossroads of “machine learning, psychiatry, and neuroscience,” with a focus on “schizophrenia and autism.” His DEI work centers on neurodiversity.

item.title: Xiang Zhou
item.description:
Xiang Zhou

Associate Professor of Sociology

Xiang Zhou is an Associate Professor of Sociology at Harvard University. His research focuses on “quantitative methodology, causes and consequences of economic inequality, and political culture in contemporary China.” He has published in several journals including Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Social Forces, Sociological Methodology, Sociological Research and Methods, and China Economic Review. Prior to Harvard, he “worked as a postdoctoral research associate at Princeton University.” He earned his PhD in Sociology and Statistics from the University of Michigan in 2015.

item.title: Xiao-Li Meng
item.description:
Xiao-Li Meng

Whipple V. N. Jones Professor of Statistics

Xiao-Li Meng is the Whipple V. N. Jones Professor and former chair of Statistics at Harvard, an Honorary Professor of the University of Hong Kong, and a faculty affiliate at the Center of Health Statistics at the University of Chicago. He is well known for his depth and breadth in research, his innovation and passion in pedagogy, and his vision and effectiveness in administration, as well as for his engaging and entertaining style as a speaker and a writer.

item.title: Xihong Lin
item.description:
Xihong Lin

Professor of Biostatistics; Professor of Statistics

Dr. Lin’s research interests lie in statistical genetics and genomics. She is interested in development and application of statistical and computational methods for analysis of high-throughput genetic, genomic and ‘omics data in epidemiological, environmental and clinical sciences, especially genetic and epigenetic epidemiology, genes and environment, and medical genomics. Current research projects include genome-wide array association studies, whole genome sequencing association studies, gene-environment interactions, and genome-wide DNA methylation studies, pathway and network analysis, and integrative genetics and genomics. She currently serves as the coordinating director of the Program of Quantitative Genomics of Harvard School of Public Heath. Her methodological work is currently supported by the MERIT award from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Methods for Correlated and High-Dimensional Biomedical Data,” and the PO1 from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Informatics in Cancer Research.” She is the contacting PI for the training grant entitled “Joint training in biostatistics and computational biology.”

item.title: Yaron Singer
item.description:
Yaron Singer

Associate in Computer Science

Yaron Singer is an Associate in Computer Science. He previously held the position of “Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at Harvard.” Before that, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Google Research and earned his PhD from UC Berkeley. His awards include the 2012 Best Student Paper Award at the ACM conference on Web Search and Data Mining, the 2010 Facebook Fellowship, the 2009 Microsoft Research Fellowship, and “several entrepreneurial awards for work on social networks.”

item.title: Yoshitaka Nishikawa
item.description:
Yoshitaka Nishikawa

Associate Professor, Kyoto University

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Yuhua Wang
item.description:
Yuhua Wang

Associate Professor of Government

He is an Associate Professor in the Department of Government at Harvard University whose research focuses on “state institutions and state-business relations in China.” He authored Tying the Autocrat’s Hands: The Rise of the Rule of Law in China (Cambridge University Press, 2015).

He earned his B.A. and M.A. from Peking University in 2003 and 2006, and his Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Michigan in 2011. From 2011 to 2015, he served as assistant professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania.

Zhichao Jiang

Professor, Sun Yat-sen University

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.
